title: US Moves to Scrap World Bank Gas Ban as Asia's LNG Buyers Face a $1bn Winter
subhead: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tells the World Bank to formally retire its decade-old ban on upstream oil and gas financing, while Pakistan warns it will pay over $1 billion for winter LNG and Europe's benchmark gas price returns to 2022 levels.

sections.heading: Washington Opens a Second Front: Attacking the World Bank's Fossil-Fuel Ban
sections.body:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent formally asked the World Bank to reverse its policy of not financing upstream oil and gas, arguing the institution 'should formally retire its prohibition on financing upstream gas and oil.' In a statement for the World Bank Development Committee and the IMF's IMFC, Bessent tied the demand to the Bank's energy-access goal of connecting 300 million more Africans, writing that reaching it 'will require the Bank to take a technology-neutral approach rather than restricting borrower choice.'

The World Bank stopped financing upstream oil and gas after 2019, with a narrow exception for upstream gas in the poorest countries. OilPrice reports the push is part of a broader Trump administration campaign to strip ESG criteria out of multilateral lenders, and comes after Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in September that the US will 'either reform the IEA or we will leave the IEA.'

This is not a drilling story so much as a governance story. The same week that Washington lobbies to free up development finance for hydrocarbons, it is also leaning on the IEA's demand forecasts. Whoever controls how the world's energy institutions model and finance supply shapes the next decade's investment map.
sections.whyItMatters: If the Bank's ban falls, it reopens a financing channel for gas projects in Africa and South Asia that has been closed since 2019 — a durable shift in who funds supply growth, not just a rhetorical win.

sections.heading: Pakistan Puts a Price on the Hormuz Squeeze: $1bn for Ten Winter Cargoes
sections.body:
The head of Pakistan LNG Limited, Masood Nabi, told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh that winter will be 'challenging' and that the binding constraint is not gas availability but disrupted transit through the Strait of Hormuz. OilPrice reports Pakistan will need to buy an additional 10 spot cargoes for November 2026 through February 2027, at roughly double the price of its Qatari term volumes — a bill in excess of $1 billion.

Context matters here: Pakistan sourced 99% of its LNG from Qatar last year. After Qatar declared force majeure in March following Iranian strikes on Ras Laffan, Pakistan was pushed into the spot market, paying what a CSIS analysis describes as high-$20s per MMBtu — versus roughly $12–13/MMBtu for Asian spot cargoes in mid-2025. CSIS notes Pakistan has already shut two fertilizer plants to redirect gas to power, with knock-on effects for rice and wheat seasons, and has leaned on diplomacy with Iran to secure safe passage for Qatari cargoes.

The pattern is Asia-wide: CSIS reports India, Bangladesh and Pakistan buying spot LNG in the low $20s per MMBtu, with India recently paying over $23. The price-sensitive buyer class has been priced out of its own protection.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the clearest illustration yet that Hormuz is now a food-and-fertilizer crisis for South Asia, not just an oil-price story — and the cost is landing on the poorest importers first.

sections.heading: Qatar's Amir Confirms the Damage: $83bn Expansion Hangs on Reopening Hormuz
sections.body:
Qatar's Amir said publicly that the Hormuz closure and attacks on gas facilities have disrupted LNG exports, per Arab Times. Behind that statement sits a hard number: Iran's March 18 strike on Ras Laffan Industrial City knocked out two of Qatar's 14 LNG trains, removing roughly 17% of national export capacity and an estimated $20 billion in annual revenue, according to newsbase and OilPrice. QatarEnergy expects those 12.8 million tons/year of capacity to stay offline three to five years.

QatarEnergy CEO Saad al-Kaabi said North Field East's first train remains on schedule for H1 2027, but further trains depend on Hormuz traffic resuming and North Field South hitting its 2028 start. Qatar entered 2026 targeting a lift from 77 to 142 million tons/year by 2030 — an $83 billion program that would have supplied about 40% of all new LNG reaching the market. Qatar is partially routing around the problem via its Golden Pass venture with ExxonMobil in Texas, with Train 2 due in H2 2026.
sections.whyItMatters: A three-to-five-year repair timeline turns a shipping crisis into a structural supply gap. The world's cheapest LNG exporter is being forced to reroute its growth through the United States.

sections.heading: Europe Enters Winter With 74% Storage and 2022-Level Prices
sections.body:
Europe's benchmark TTF gas price sits at $96.56 (€86.03) per MWh, its highest since December 2022, OilPrice reports. EU storage was only 74% full as of October 14, per Gas Infrastructure Europe data, against a five-year average of about 86% for the date.

The asymmetry is striking: oil flows out of the Persian Gulf have partially recovered, but Middle East LNG flows remain about 80% below last year's volumes, ING's Warren Patterson noted Thursday. 'The market is increasingly accepting that Persian Gulf LNG could remain largely absent from global markets for much of the Northern Hemisphere winter,' Patterson wrote.

Timera Energy's winter outlook assumes Hormuz stays closed through Q4 2026 with gradual reopening in Q1 2027, and flags late-winter price spikes as 'particularly acute if European stocks run low.' Europe and Asia are now bidding against each other for the same shrinking pool of spot cargoes.
sections.whyItMatters: With buffers thin and demand-side flexibility largely exhausted in Asia, the price risk is concentrated in late winter — a cold January could force a second round of industrial demand destruction in Europe.

sections.heading: The Evasion Map Redraws Itself: Ship-to-Ship Transfers Move to India's West Coast
sections.body:
Vortexa vessel-tracking data cited by The National shows 82 cargoes, about 680,000 barrels per day, were transferred ship-to-ship onto larger vessels in India's Gulf of Kutch in September. The waters off Hormuz have become so congested with STS operations that the activity has spilled as far east as India's west coast, because the nearest zones off Fujairah (UAE) and Sohar (Oman) are hitting operational limits.

Vortexa senior analyst Varaleka Pant told The National that the transfer itself is relatively low-risk — 'the real risk lies in getting the barrels out of the west of Hormuz to the STS zone.' The pricing reflects that: Iraq is offering Basrah Medium at a $34.50/barrel discount and Basrah Heavy at a $37 discount to regional benchmarks, because Baghdad has no bypass route. The UAE, by contrast, earns a premium for Murban crude, which reaches Fujairah via pipeline outside the Strait.
sections.whyItMatters: The discounts prove that route optionality — not geology — now sets the value of a barrel. Producers with a pipeline bypass capture a premium; those without one pay tens of dollars per barrel to move crude at all.

sections.heading: The US Diesel License Meets Reality: Russia Strikes Ukraine's Grid
sections.body:
Four days after the Trump administration licensed imports of Russian diesel, Russian strikes on October 13–14 cut power to at least 600,000 Ukrainians, President Zelenskyy said. He reported 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones aimed at Kyiv and Kharkiv, damaging at least 26 power facilities and four oil and gas sites. A ballistic missile hit Kyiv's CHP-4 plant; Russia's Defense Ministry said it struck seven Ukrainian energy facilities and a data center.

The diplomatic backdrop is muddled and worth noting precisely. Trump announced an 'energy ceasefire' on October 11 that Zelenskyy denied and the Kremlin did not confirm; a White House official told Axios it covered only refineries, 'refinery for refinery.' CNN reported Washington warned Kyiv it could suspend intelligence sharing and European weapons purchases if Ukraine did not halt strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. The Treasury's General License 135 authorizing Russian-origin diesel runs to April 7, 2027, and does not authorize debits to accounts of Russia's central bank, National Wealth Fund or Finance Ministry.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is simultaneously easing sanctions on Russian fuel and pressing Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries, while Russia escalates strikes on Ukraine's grid — a contradiction that tells you Washington's priority is domestic fuel prices, not battlefield leverage.

sections.heading: Nuclear Fuel: Urenco Hits 75% as Russia Still Controls Half of Enrichment
sections.body:
Urenco USA said its National Enrichment Facility in Eunice, New Mexico, is three-quarters through its expansion, with the sixth of eight centrifuge cascades now producing. OilPrice reports the plant holds 4.3 million SWU of capacity — about one-third of US enriched uranium demand — and is adding 700,000 SWU through the project, targeting over 7 million SWU within a decade.

The geopolitical stakes are set by the World Nuclear Association's estimate that Russia controls nearly half of global enrichment capacity, against uranium demand projected to rise 28% by 2030. US demand growth is being driven in part by AI data-center loads. Separately, World Nuclear News reports Singapore is 'seriously studying' deployment of small modular reactors — a signal that the Iran war's exposure of import dependence is pushing even risk-averse Asian states toward nuclear.
sections.whyItMatters: Enrichment is the one nuclear chokepoint that is genuinely hard to substitute, and the US remains roughly two-thirds dependent on others for it. Each cascade that starts up in New Mexico is a small reduction in Russian leverage.

bottomLine: Today's developments point the same direction from different angles: the Hormuz crisis is hardening into a multi-year structural problem and the world is reorganizing around it. Qatar confirms damage that takes three to five years to repair; Europe enters winter with 74% storage and gas at 2022 prices; Pakistan faces a $1bn bill for ten winter cargoes; and the evasion economy has physically relocated to India's west coast. Meanwhile Washington is fighting on the institutional level — pushing the World Bank to scrap its upstream oil and gas ban while licensing Russian diesel and pressing Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries. The through-line is that the US is now prioritizing price relief and supply access over climate architecture and battlefield pressure alike. Watch the World Bank vote and Europe's late-winter storage trajectory as the next two pressure points.
sources: OilPrice.com, CSIS, The National (Abu Dhabi), Arab Times, ING (via think.ing.com), Timera Energy, Gas Infrastructure Europe (AGSI), Vortexa, newsbase, QatarEnergy, Urenco USA, World Nuclear Association, World Nuclear News, CNN, Axios, Euronews, Al Jazeera, Irish Times, ABC News, Kyiv Independent, US Treasury, Reuters
